_README: THE SAME-RATIO PAIR, AND THE SOLVE IT COMPLETES.
20/40 and 32.5/65 hold the same 1:2 front-to-rear ratio at nearly double
the magnitude. They read 0.54 and 0.56. Different — so Mechanical Balance
is NOT a pure ratio, there are additive terms, and the model fitted
yesterday to four rows had something real to be fitted to.
With these two rows there are six independent settings on one car and only
three free parameters. The model is overdetermined by three and it matches
ALL SIX to the last printed digit. See solvedModel.

held.note: springs returned to the app's prescribed values before this pair, so these rows share a hold-point with rows 1-4 of balance-mb-gr86-2026-08-12.json

rows.purpose: SAME-RATIO PAIR (a) — first attempt, caught mid-SIMULATING

sameRatioPairResult: 20/40 reads 0.54. 32.5/65 reads 0.56. SAME RATIO, DIFFERENT READOUT.
Mechanical Balance therefore depends on the absolute size of the bars, not
only on their ratio. Every pure-ratio model is dead — which is what this
pair was designed to decide, and it decided it in two readings exactly as
solvedModel: MECHANICAL BALANCE IS SOLVED ON THIS CAR.
MB = R / (F + R)
F = arF + 0.150 x spF + 50.5
R = arR + 0.150 x spR + 72.3
Bars in slider points, springs in lb/in. Read as a roll-stiffness split
where the REAR share is what the game prints.
EVERY ROW MEASURED ON THIS CAR, against the model:
arF/arR      spF/spR        model    printed
Six settings, three free parameters (the spring weight and the two axle
constants; the bar weight is the scale and is fixed at 1). Overdetermined
by three, and every row lands on the printed digit.
AND TWO ROWS IT WAS NOT FITTED TO:
The app's own tune is a clean independent hit. The game's default tune
misses by a single rounding step, and it is the one row taken at a
different ride height (4.4/4.8 against 4.2/4.4) and a different tire
pressure (31.0 against 31.5) — both of which are inside the axle constants.
So the residual points at exactly the terms that were held constant
everywhere else, which is the good kind of miss.
WHAT THE COEFFICIENTS MEAN:
- ONE BAR POINT IS WORTH ABOUT 6.7 lb/in OF SPRING. Bars run 1-65 and
springs a few hundred, so across their full ranges the two have
comparable authority over the balance. That is why neither a bars-only
nor a springs-only model could ever have fitted.
- THE AXLE CONSTANTS ARE LARGE AND REAR-BIASED, 50.5 front against 72.3
rear, together about 40% of the total. They are the tires, the geometry
and the unsprung mass — everything that resists roll without being on a
slider. They are why equal bars and a front-stiff spring pair still
read above 0.5.
- THEY ALSO ABSORB TIRE PRESSURE, which is why 31.5 -> 50 psi moved MB
0.51 -> 0.50 with nothing else touched.
whatThisIsWorthToTheApp: The app currently prints a target band of 0.55-0.65 and its own tune lands
at 0.51, with no indication of which way to move or by how much. With MB
solved that becomes an exact instruction — but the coefficients above are
THIS CAR'S, and 50.5 / 72.3 / 0.150 encode its tires, geometry and weight
distribution. They will not transfer.
THE FIX THAT NEEDS NO PER-CAR CONSTANTS, and it is better than a formula:
MB is smooth and monotonic in the bar settings, so two readings calibrate
any car in about thirty seconds.
1. read MB at the tune's bars
2. add 10 to the rear bar, read MB again
3. the difference is that car's sensitivity per bar point; scale it to
the distance to target and set the bar
ON THIS CAR, from the model rather than from arithmetic done in a hurry:
at the app's tune   F = 152.0, R = 158.6, MB = 0.5106
add 10 rear         R = 168.6, MB = 0.5259    -> 0.0153 per 10 points
to reach 0.55       R must be 186.0           -> +27 rear bar
CORRECTED 2026-08-12, same day: an earlier version of this block said
'about 0.028 per 10 points' and '+14 rear'. Both were wrong — the figure
was estimated off two rows by eye instead of differentiated from the model
sitting directly above it. The error mattered: +14 lands at about 0.53 and
would have left a user short of the band while believing they had followed
the instruction. Recorded rather than silently fixed, because the lesson is
that a solved model makes eyeballing unnecessary and therefore inexcusable.
So the app can print a concrete number derived from the user's own car
rather than a band derived from constants measured on a GR86.
It also finally makes the Verify In Game section honest. It has been
telling users to hit a Mechanical Balance target using the bars, which is
the right lever — but the app's own tune misses the band it prints, and
until now nothing could say by how much or in which direction.
stillOwed: ONE CAR. The structure — rear share, bars and springs both in, large
additive axle terms — should generalise because it is roll stiffness. The
three coefficients should not, because they are the car.
The cheapest test of the structure is three readings on a second car:
equal bars, then the same-ratio pair. If MB is still the rear share and
the pair still splits, the form holds and only the numbers change.
Ride height is untested and sits inside the axle constants on this
evidence. Rows 6 and 7 of MEASURE.md Phase 1 — ride height at fixed bars —
are now worth taking, since the model predicts they will move MB and by
notes: Lateral G was 1.26 and 1.42 on every row again. Across this sweep, the previous sweep and the pressure row, that is now five separate tune changes — bars, springs, pressure, gearing, aero — with only aero moving it. Case S5's answer is looking like a firm no: lateral G is a compound-and-aero readout, not a tune readout, and grip-side constants stay lap-times-only.
